title: Four regression alerts, zero regressions
summary: The board flagged four regressions in four days — Gemini 3.5 Flash -11.4, Grok 4.3 -5.7, Llama 3.3 70B -2.9, Gemini 3.1 Pro -2.9. None of them was a model getting worse. Two were failed calls; two were a single question.

body.p: Between 21 and 24 July the scheduled probe opened four regression alerts. Every one of them was auto-logged with the same warning — confirm it's real before writing it up. Here is what confirming looked like, and why none of the four became a post.
Start with the two big ones. Both are Google, and both come with a reliability drop in the same run:

body.code:
gemini-3.5-flash  22 Jul  acc 1.000  reliability 1.000
                  23 Jul  acc 0.886  reliability 0.914   <- -11.4 pts

gemini-3.1-pro    22 Jul  acc 0.914  reliability 0.943
                  23 Jul  acc 0.886  reliability 0.914   <- -2.9 pts
                  24 Jul  acc 0.971  reliability 1.000   <- rebounds

body.p: Reliability is the share of calls that came back at all. When it falls with accuracy, the probe failed, not the model — a call that never returned is scored as a wrong answer, which is exactly the failure mode this board documented on 20 July when Groq's rate limit took Llama to 3%. Gemini 3.1 Pro settles it: the next clean run came back at 97.1%, higher than before the 'regression'. Nothing regressed; some calls didn't land.
The other two are cleaner and more interesting, because reliability stayed at 1.000 the whole time — those numbers are real:

The suite is 35 frozen tasks. One task is 100/35 = 2.86 points. So -2.9 points is one question changing its answer, and -5.7 is two. Those aren't regressions; they're the smallest movement the instrument can register. A 35-task suite cannot resolve anything finer than about three points, and reporting a one-question flip as a model regression would be reading noise as signal.

So: four alerts, four days, zero posts. Two artifacts and two single-question flips. The alerting is doing its job — it is supposed to be sensitive, and a tracker that only fires on catastrophes misses real drift. But sensitivity is only useful if something downstream is willing to say no, which is why the stub the probe writes tells its own author to go check the run log and the reliability metric first.

The uncomfortable version: the most common output of a drift tracker is a false positive. Publishing 'Gemini regressed 11 points' would have been fast, legible, and wrong — about a named company's model, in public. The measurement that matters most here isn't any model's accuracy. It's the share of my own alerts that survive checking, and this week that share was zero.

title: The drift that was a rate limit
summary: Llama 3.3 70B "dropped" 66 points overnight. It was Groq's 30 RPM cap, not the model — and a rate limit scoring as 0% looks exactly like the thing this board exists to catch.

body.p: On 2026-07-20 the board showed Llama 3.3 70B fall from 69% to 3%, and Llama 3.1 8B to 0% — overnight, on a frozen suite. That is a regression post. It wasn't drift.
The run log told the real story:

body.code:
api.groq.com -> 429: Rate limit reached for model `llama-3.3-70b-versatile`
service tier `on_demand` ... requests per minute (RPM): Limit 30, Used 30

body.p: 34 of 35 calls, both Llama models, were rate-limited. They run on Groq's free tier — 30 RPM shared across the org — and probing two models back-to-back spent the budget. Every 429'd call scored as a wrong answer, so accuracy cratered toward zero. Google threw a few 503s and xAI a 429 too, same category.

The model didn't get dumber; a rate limit scored as a 0%. And a rate limit scoring as a 0% is the single most misleading thing a drift tracker can do — it looks exactly like the thing it exists to catch. Switch to the Reliability metric (button below) and you can see it: the share of calls that succeeded fell off a cliff for those two models, which is the honest signal that the probe, not the model, failed.

The board already tracked reliability separately and left the failed probes out of the auto-written summary, so it never claimed a regression. But the accuracy chart still dove toward 0, and there was no retry. So the probe was hardened: retry 429/5xx honoring Retry-After, throttle each provider to its rate cap, and drop points below a reliability floor from the accuracy line. Reliability keeps the dip — that's the true signal.
The hard part of an eval board isn't detecting drift. It's not manufacturing it. The most valuable thing the board did that week was stop a post from going out.
